standard.title: Historical Interpretations and Debates in the Late 20th Century
standard.description: different historical interpretations and debates during the second half of the 20th century
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied historical interpretations and debates about WWI and the interwar period at Year 9 level.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students discuss significant historical interpretations and debates from the second half of the 20th century, including First Nations cultural assertiveness, global rights movements, extremism, nuclear energy, and climate change.

nodes.label: First Nations cultural assertiveness and global rights movements
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss how First Nations Australians became more assertive in developing their own cultural industries and explain the significance of global rights movements in the second half of the 20th century.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe how First Nations Australians became more assertive in developing their cultural industries and discuss at least two significant global rights movements of the late 20th century.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss the concept of popular culture and how First Nations Australians became more assertive in developing their own arts industries — examining the role of Bangarra Dance Theatre in advancing First Nations cultures, beliefs, stories and concerns through dance and music; discuss significant global rights movements: the US Civil Rights movement, the rights movement of First Nations Peoples of Australia, South Africa's anti-apartheid movement, women's movements, LGBTQI+ movements and environmental movements; examine how these movements interacted and influenced each other.
wider: Investigate the development of First Nations Australian arts industries in depth — examining how artists like Albert Namatjira, the Papunya Tula artists, and Bangarra Dance Theatre navigated the intersection of cultural sovereignty, commercial recognition, and political advocacy

Examine the global anti-apartheid movement as a case study in international solidarity — analysing how boycotts, diplomacy, and internal resistance combined to produce the end of apartheid, and what Australia's role in the movement reveals about how Australian values shaped foreign policy

response_modes.reason: Global rights movements are most productively taught comparatively — examining how different movements used similar strategies (direct action, legal challenge, international solidarity, cultural expression) in different national contexts. The Australian First Nations movement connects directly to K09–K13.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The global rights movement comparison offers a rich opportunity to examine how historical struggles for rights have operated across different legal, cultural and political contexts — developing the comparative historical thinking directly relevant to S07.
success_criteria: Describe how First Nations Australians became more assertive in developing their cultural industries, using at least one specific example
Identify at least two significant global rights movements of the late 20th century and explain the main goals of each
Explain how at least two global rights movements influenced or reinforced each other

nodes.label: Extremism, nuclear energy, and climate change debates
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the rise of political and religious extremism, and discuss the evolving debates over nuclear energy and climate change from the 1960s to the present.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the impact of at least one significant act of political or religious extremism on Australian society and explain how the debates over nuclear energy or climate change have changed over time.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the rise of political and religious extremism and its impact on immigration to Australia — including the events of 11 September 2001 and the 2002 Bali bombings and their effects on immigration policy, security measures, and attitudes to Muslim communities; discuss the global debate over nuclear energy from the 1960s to the present — arguments for and against its use as an alternative to fossil fuels, and the effects of nuclear disasters (Three Mile Island 1979, Chernobyl 1986, Fukushima Daiichi 2011); investigate the change in debate about climate change from the 1960s to the present.
wider: Examine the historiography of the climate change debate — tracing how the scientific consensus developed from the 1970s, how it entered public and political discourse, and why it became politicised in the 1990s–2000s, comparing Australia's trajectory with that of other countries

Investigate the Fukushima Daiichi disaster (2011) in depth as a case study in how a single event can reshape public opinion on nuclear energy — examining the gap between scientific risk assessment and public perception, and how different countries responded differently to the same event

response_modes.reason: These are genuinely contested debates where evidence, values, and political interests interact. Model the distinction between 'what the scientific evidence shows' and 'how the evidence has been interpreted and disputed in public debate' — both are historically significant and require different analytical approaches.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The climate change and nuclear energy debates are paradigm cases for examining how historical interpretation is shaped by the interaction of evidence, values, and political interests — directly relevant to S07 (contested historical interpretations) and to the broader question of how societies respond to scientific knowledge.
success_criteria: Describe the impact of at least one significant act of extremism on Australian immigration policy or social attitudes
Explain how the debate over nuclear energy has changed since the 1960s, identifying at least one event that shifted the debate
Describe how the climate change debate has evolved from the 1960s to the present, explaining what drove the key shifts
